extracted.intended_audience: journalism scholars, media researchers, newsroom editors, and journalists interested in news selection practices
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and mechanisms reporters and editors use to select and publish news in competitive online and print newsrooms, emphasizing monitoring, imitation, and real-time metrics. Useful for analyzing newsroom decision-making and the drivers of content homogeneity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competitor coverage / adoption
rubrics_metrics.description: What competitors are covering — an explicit imitation signal; competitor adoption (e.g., if the NYT covered it, others must) drives selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists monitor rival outlets and treat stories covered by major competitors as signals to cover the same item. This produces pile-on dynamics; failure to follow competitor adoption can be seen as a competitive disadvantage. Reliance on competitor coverage tends to produce content homogeneity across outlets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trending topics / real-time virality
rubrics_metrics.description: What's already trending — real-time virality and 'what's trending' guide selection; items that are going viral or generating clicks are more likely to be picked up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newsrooms follow trending topics and social buzz as a selection shortcut. This encourages amplification of already-popular stories (pile-on) and privileges items that attract immediate attention over less-visible but potentially important reporting. Editors may prioritize stories expected to generate high short-term traffic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowns over unknowns / source familiarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Preference for established sources and familiar facts rather than unknowns or novel sources; 'knowns over unknowns' and 'source familiarity' influence story choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters favor stories that rely on familiar institutions, official sources, and predictable beats because they are easier/safer to cover and verify quickly. This bias reduces the likelihood of coverage of new voices or uncertain claims and can limit investigative or original reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Real-time competitive pressures (dashboards, hourly checks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Real-time competitive pressures — use of dashboards, hourly checks, and constant monitoring shapes moment-to-moment editorial choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technologies and routines (dashboards, frequent editorial check-ins) create temporal pressures that push newsrooms toward rapid, imitative decisions. These processes prioritize speed and visibility, often at the expense of depth or novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience analytics / clicks
rubrics_metrics.description: Audience analytics — metrics on what is being clicked and consumed guide selection decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors and reporters use analytics to prioritize stories that attract engagement. This metric-driven selection can privilege easily monetizable or attention-grabbing stories and distort news values toward short-term audience appeal rather than public-interest reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Established beat sources versus new voices
rubrics_metrics.description: Preference for established beat sources as opposed to elevating new voices or sources outside regular beats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newsrooms rely on an existing set of sources tied to beats, which streamlines reporting but narrows the range of perspectives covered. New or unconventional sources are less likely to be pursued because they require more verification work and risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convenience / easy availability
rubrics_metrics.description: Convenience and easy availability of information or sources influence story selection; easily accessible stories are preferred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resource limits and time pressure make readily available stories (press releases, agency copy, predictable statements) more attractive. This convenience bias reduces incentives for original reporting that demands more effort or time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beat fit
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a story 'fits' a reporter's existing assignment or beat influences whether it will be covered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors and reporters are prone to select stories that align with existing beats because they match expertise and routines. 'Beat fit' acts as a gatekeeper, channeling coverage into established topical areas and discouraging cross-beat or novel investigations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Politicians with illiberal politics (newsworthiness bias)
rubrics_metrics.description: Politicians with illiberal politics are disproportionately covered according to observed selection practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Certain actor types—here, politicians exhibiting illiberal tendencies—attract outsized attention, indicating value-laden biases in perceived newsworthiness. This prioritization can skew public attention and reinforce specific political narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hard-news vs. soft-news differential in monitoring and imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Hard-news journalists engage in more intense competitive monitoring, greater technology use, and more imitation; soft-news journalists display less imitation — making hard news most homogenized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The extent of imitation and the tools used vary by beat: hard-news beats are more susceptible to rapid monitoring and copying, amplifying homogeneity in those areas. Assessment of selection practices should account for beat-specific norms and technological adoption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality and diversity of coverage (negative/quality metric)
rubrics_metrics.description: Original reporting is reduced as imitation is rewarded; the result is homogenization and reduced diversity in audiences' news diets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use originality/diversity as an evaluative criterion: high reliance on imitation, analytics, and convenience typically correlates with lower originality and narrower coverage. Editors aiming to improve public-interest outcomes should weigh originality against short-term competitive signals.
